finalText:
**Merge** combines two branches and keeps both histories intact — you end up with a commit that says "these two branches came together here." The history shows that the work happened in parallel.

**Rebase** replays one branch's changes on top of another, rewriting history to look like the work happened in sequence instead. No merge commit, just a straight line.

**When to merge:** You're pulling someone else's work into a shared branch (main, release), or you want to preserve the fact that work happened on different paths. Safe because you're not rewriting history anyone else depends on.

**When to rebase:** You're working on your own feature branch and want to catch up with changes on main before you're done — rebase keeps your branch clean and easy to review. Also good right before you push your own changes to a shared branch, to give reviewers a linear diff. Never rebase commits you've already pushed to a shared branch (you'd rewrite history others might have built on, causing chaos).

The tradeoff: merge is safer and shows the real story of how things evolved; rebase is cleaner but rewrites history, so use it only on commits that are yours alone.
